topic: Myth: more megapixels = better photos. At viewing size (phone, Instagram, 4K TV) 12 vs 48 MP look the same; smaller pixels are noisier per pixel but equal at the same output size; megapixels pay off only for heavy crops and big close-up prints.
lines: Trick question. On a phone, they look the same.
Instagram shows photos at most ten eighty pixels wide.
Instagram shows photos at most 1080 pixels wide.
That's under one and a half megapixels.
Even a 4K TV is only eight point three.
Real simulation. Same sensor, four times the pixels.
Each pixel catches a quarter of the light...
so up close, each one is twice as noisy.
But shrink it to the same size, and the noise averages out.
Megapixels win when you crop hard...
or print big. Twenty by thirty inches, at three hundred pixels per inch, needs fifty-four megapixels.
or print big. 20 × 30 inches, at 300 pixels per inch, needs 54 megapixels.
Not cropping? Not printing? Then tell me...

youtube.title: Which Photo Is 48 Megapixels? (The Megapixel Myth)
youtube.description:
More megapixels don't make a better-looking photo at the size you actually view it. Instagram shows photos at most 1080 px wide (a 1080 x 1350 portrait is ~1.46 MP); a 4K UHD TV (3840 x 2160) is ~8.3 MP. A 12 MP and a 48 MP file look the same there.
Real numpy simulation: one optical image, sampled by the same-size sensor at 12 MP-equivalent and 48 MP-equivalent (4x the pixels, each catching 1/4 of the light). Per pixel, the 48 MP version has half the signal-to-noise ratio (photon shot noise ~ sqrt(photons)): twice as noisy at 100%. Shrunk to the same output size, averaging 4 pixels recovers the same SNR as the big pixels.
Where megapixels do pay off: heavy cropping, and big prints viewed up close. 300 ppi is a common close-viewing print guideline: 20 x 30 in x 300 ppi = 6000 x 9000 px = 54 MP (big prints seen from further away need less).
Sources: Instagram Help Center (photo resolution); Wikipedia '4K resolution'; Fstoppers 'Pixel pitch: does camera pixel size actually matter?'; digifotostarter.nl '300 dpi: what does it mean for your photo?'.
